Article https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-64650-1 How augmin establishes the angle of the microtubule branch site

Sophie M. Travis1,4,6, Jodi Kraus1,6, Collin T. McManus 1,5, Kiana Golden 2, Rui Zhang 3 & Sabine Petry 1

How microtubules (MTs) are generated in the proper orientation is essential to understanding how the cytoskeleton organizes a cell and MT-dependent events such as cell division. In the spindle, most MTs are generated through the branching MT nucleation pathway. In this pathway, new MTs are nucleated from the side of existing MTs and oriented at a shallow angle by the branching factor augmin, ensuring that both MTs have the same polarity. Yet, how augmin binds MTs and sets the branch angle has remained unclear. Here, we report the cryo-electron microscopy structure of an augmin subcomplex on the MT. This structure resembles that of NDC80 bound to the MT, with the conserved CH domain of augmin’s Haus6 subunit directly proximal to the MT lattice. We ﬁnd that the Haus6 CH domain is a bona ﬁde MT binding site that increases augmin’s afﬁnity for the MT and helps establish branch angle. A second binding site, located in the disordered N-terminus of Haus8, also establishes branch angle,. Thus, we ﬁnd that augmin regulates MT branching using two domains, each tuned to modulate MT afﬁnity and MT branch angle. This work expands our mechanistic understanding of branching MT nucleation and thus spindle formation.

Microtubules (MTs) are a primary component of the eukaryotic cytoskeleton, where they play critical roles in organellar and vesicular trafﬁcking, cellular motility, and, during cell division, chromosome segregation. For each of these roles, new MTs must be generated on demand in real-time through MT nucleation. Moreover, the polarity of new MTs must be strictly controlled to ensure that cargos and chromosomes are correctly trafﬁcked. MT nucleation proceeds through multiple biochemical pathways, and one of the most important during spindle assembly is branching MT nucleation1–4. New branched daughter MTs emanate at a shallow angle, generally between 0° and 30°, and share the same polarity of the pre-existing mother MTs5,6. Thus, on the micron scale, branching MT nucleation preserves spindle MT polarity. Several MT-associated proteins (MAPs) have been shown to promote branching MT nucleation6–8. However, in its simplest form,

branching MT nucleation requires only two protein complexes: the universal MT nucleator γ-TuRC and the branching-speciﬁc heterooctameric augmin complex9–11. Augmin’s primary function in branching MT nucleation is to recruit γ-TuRC to pre-existing MTs12,13. Moreover, augmin appears to establish the overall architecture of the MT branch site, as reconstitution of MT branching with only augmin and γ- TuRC recapitulates the shallow branch angles observed in endogenous branching9–11,14. Yet, how augmin orients γ-TuRC and the daughter MT of the resulting branch has remained unclear. Recent experimental models of both human and Xenopus laevis augmin, determined using single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (EM), have provided the groundwork to answer this question14–16. These models demonstrated that augmin is a relatively rigid complex, composed of a γ-TuRC-binding stalk (T-III) and an arch (T-II) that binds the pre-existing MT12,13,17. thus made the complex seem a good candidate to enforce a deﬁned range of angles between γ-TuRC and the pre-existing MT, one major issue remained. Prior biochemical data had implicated the N-terminus of T-II subunit Haus8, a low-complexity, highly electropositive 150- residue sequence, as the primary MT binding region (MTBR) within the complex12,18. Yet, no electron density corresponding to this region could be found in any of the experimental datasets, presumably due to inherent ﬂexibility14–16. This begs the question: if augmin connects to the pre-existing MT only via a ﬂexible, unstructured region, how can augmin possibly impose global structure on the branch site and deﬁne the range of branch angles. To answer this question, in this work, we report the cryo-electron microscopy structure of an augmin subcomplex bound to the MT lattice. Our prior structures had found that augmin contains two CH domains, which are often MT binding regions. The structure of augmin on the MT reveals that the CH domain of Haus6 is, in fact, a bona ﬁde MT binding region. Using structure-based biochemistry, we characterize the role of the MT binding regions and uncover how augmin regulates MT binding and branching angle, which is important for its function in the spindle during cell division.

Results Engineering augmin T-IIbonsai To understand how augmin interacts with the lattice of the mother MT, we needed to obtain the structure of augmin bound to the MT. Prior work from our lab and others12,13 established that full-length augmin can be visualized sparsely decorating MTs. However, it was not possible to produce full-length augmin above the dissociation constant of 1 μM previously reported12, making it infeasible to saturate the MT lattice with full-length augmin, as would be required for single particle cryo-EM. Thus, we explored truncations of the augmin complex, as well as subcomplexes, to identify a more tractable structural target. Our prior structure of X. laevis augmin14 suggested that both the MTBR of Haus8, as well as the putative MT-binding CH domains of Haus6 and Haus7 were clustered at the N-terminus of tetramer T-II (Fig. 1a). Using the augmin structure as a guide, we located an internal hinge at the apex of T-II (Fig. 1a, Supplementary Fig. 1a, b). We truncated T-II at this hinge and were able to produce a shortened T-II that we termed augmin T-IIbonsai (Fig. 1a, Supplementary Fig. 1a, b). Surprisingly, Haus2 was excluded from the complex upon puriﬁcation (Supplementary Fig. 1c). This is consistent with the more transient association of Haus2 with T-II that we had previously reported13. Nonetheless, the Haus6/Haus7/Haus8 heterotrimeric subcomplex was predicted to still form a folded, albeit remodeled, heterotrimer that, crucially, maintains the same architecture of the MT-binding regions as the full-length complex (Supplementary Fig. 1d). Furthermore, the complex was highly soluble and could be produced at a concentration of 10 μM. Using MT pelleting assays, we determined the afﬁnity of T-IIbonsai for the MT lattice as 200 ± 80 nM (Supplementary Fig. 5a, b), in line with the previously reported afﬁnity of the full length complex12. Thus, we established that T-IIbonsai was a promising target for structural studies on the MT lattice.

Structure of augmin T-IIbonsai on the MT To determine the structure of augmin T-IIbonsai bound to the MT lattice, we prepared grids of GMPCPP-stabilized MTs, then ﬂowed in the augmin T-IIbonsai construct before grid blotting and freezing. After screening for coated MTs (Supplementary Fig. 6), data collection (Supplementary Table 1), and data processing (Supplementary Fig. 6), we obtained a reconstruction of the 14-protoﬁlament GMPCPP-stabilized MT decorated with density corresponding to T-IIbonsai at 3.8 Å resolution (Fig. 1b, Supplementary Fig. 6). Symmetry expansion followed by further reﬁnement led to a reconstruction of a single tubulin dimer bound to a single copy of T-IIbonsai at 3.1 Å resolution (Fig. 1c). The highest resolution region of the map corresponded to the MT

lattice (Supplementary Fig. 7a, b), however, the resolution of the T-IIbonsai density, ranging from 3 to 5 Å, was sufﬁcient to interpret the structure of T-IIbonsai bound to the MT. Although in the full augmin structure, T-IIbonsai forms a rigid unit, in our structure, only a portion of the T-IIbonsai is visible. This portion consists of a single CH domain, closest to the MT lattice, and an adjacent stalk region, composed of three α-helices, that points away from the lattice (Fig. 1d). This stalk is the precise length of the α-helical trimer at the N-terminus of T-II prior to incorporation of the Haus2 α- helix into a tetrameric bundle (Supplementary Fig. 8a). Thus, we may observe ordered density for only a portion of the complex because, in the absence of Haus2, the remainder fails to fold. Rigid-body docking of the N-terminus of T-II into the density was most consistent with Haus6 contributing the ordered CH domain, rather than Haus7, as this allowed for correct positioning of the α-helical stalk (Supplementary Fig. 8a, b). Furthermore, docking of the predicted structure of the Haus6 CH domain appropriately positions many bulky aromatic residues within the density (Supplementary Fig. 8c, d). These bulky residues are generally not conserved between Haus6 and Haus7 (Supplementary Fig. 8e), so this provides further agreement with our assignment of the Haus6 CH domain as closest to the MT lattice. Our structure shows a modest binding surface between augmin and the MT lattice (Fig. 2a), with a buried surface area of 664 Å2. A little under half of the binding surface (309 Å2) contacts α-tubulin, mediated by αB’ and αE loop of Haus6 (Fig. 2a, Supplementary Fig. 9a). In addition, the short αF helix of Haus6, although down weighted by the deep-learning driven sharpening algorithm deepEMhancer, is visible in close proximity to β-tubulin in traditionally, globally-sharpened map (Supplementary Fig. 9b, c), and contributes an additional 355 Å2 of buried surface area. In addition to the CH domain of Haus6, augmin has been proposed to contain two other MT binding sites: the CH domain of Haus716

and the MTBR of Haus812,18 As discussed above, the CH domain of Haus7 is not visible in our structure; however, its position can be inferred by docking larger fragments of augmin into our map (Supplementary Fig. 8a). Thus, our structure implies that the Haus7 CH domain may not directly contact the MT lattice. Surprisingly, we observe no additional density in our map that could correspond to the Haus8 N-terminal MTBR (Supplementary Fig. 10a, b). As the highly electronegative tails of α- and β-tubulin are predicted to be adjacent to the location to the Haus8 MTBR (Fig. 2a), we speculate that Haus8’s N-terminal electropositive MTBR may contribute to electrostatic attraction to the tubulin tails, thus enhancing augmin’s MT binding afﬁnity without displaying appreciable ordered binding. Previous studies have shown that augmin shows substantial afﬁnity for the tubulin tails19, and similar phenomena have been previously reported for regions of many electropositive MAPs, such as tau20 and NDC8021,22.

Roles of the bipartite binding interface in MT binding afﬁnity From our structure, the Haus6 CH domain appears to be wellpositioned to interact with the tubulin lattice (Fig. 2a). Moreover, the surface adjacent to the tubulin dimer is both conserved and electropositive (Fig. 2b). Thus, we hypothesized that the Haus6 CH domain could contribute to augmin’s MT binding afﬁnity. We tested this hypothesis by assessing which regions of augmin are necessary for MT binding. We generated augmin mutants that were missing the Haus8 MTBR or the Haus6 CH domain, as well as a mutant missing the Haus7 CH domain. Next, we visualized the binding of augmin mutants to immobilized, ﬂuorescently labeled GMPCPP MT seeds via total internal reﬂection (TIRF) microscopy. As expected, wildtype augmin displayed robust binding to the MT seeds (Fig. 2c). Previous work using human augmin suggested that deletion of the Haus8 MTBR was sufﬁcient to abrogate MT binding of the entire complex12. However, when we deleted the Haus8 MTBR from X. laevis augmin, we found that MT binding was weakened but not abolished (Fig. 2c, d). Similarly, puriﬁed

MT lattice preference of branching factors As described above, T-II and NDC80 have marked structural and biochemical similarities in how the complexes bind to MTs. Yet, one major difference between the two complexes is their localization on the MT. The NDC80 complex, in its role of capturing MT plus ends at the kinetochore, prefers and tracks the lattice at the growing MT plus end23. In contrast, augmin tends to localize along the entire MT and enable branching MT nucleation uniformly along its length. Moreover, augmin has not been reported to have any plus-end tracking activity, either in vitro, in X. laevis egg extract, or in vivo. Therefore, we investigated whether augmin’s localization could be explained by a preference for a speciﬁc nucleotide state of the MT lattice. To directly investigate augmin’s lattice preference, we employed two variations on a dual-lattice TIRF microscopy binding assay, inspired by Mauer et al. and Zhang et al. 28,29. In the ﬁrst variation, we initially nucleated Atto 647N-labeled GMPCPP MT seeds, then performed another round of polymerization with Alexa568 tubulin and GTPγS. The resulting MTs had regions that mimic the GTP MT lattice (GMPCPP), at the plus end, and the GDP + Pi transition state (GTPγS), further from the plus end, each labeled with a distinct ﬂuorophore. As a proof of concept, we incubated seeds with EB1 and found, as previously reported, that the protein preferred the GTPγS lattice over GMPCPP (Fig. 3a, b, Supplementary Fig. 13)26,29. The branching factor TPX2 has been previously reported to prefer GMPCPP lattice30, and we also recapitulated this preference for the GMPCPP lattice (Fig. 3a, b, Supplementary Fig. 13). Having shown that proteins can preferentially localize to both lattice types in our system, we next assayed augmin’s lattice preference. We found that augmin, like EB1, strongly prefers the GTPγS lattice over GMPCPP (Fig. 3a, b), suggesting that, consistent with prior observations, augmin does not preferentially bind lattice found at the plus-end11,31. In addition, augmin lacking the MTBR of Haus8 maintains its preference for GTPγS lattice over GMPCPP, suggesting that lattice preference is encoded in the Haus6 CH domain (Fig. 3a, b). Prior experiments using dynamic MTs found preferential accumulation of augmin and other branching factors on older lattice. This could be due to slow kinetics of augmin accumulation or, alternatively, a preference for GDP lattice. Thus, we next asked whether augmin displayed any preference for GDP lattice over the other types. To address this question, we modiﬁed our lattice preference conditions by mixing the above-described GMPCPP-GTPγS MTs with orthogonally-colored dynamic MTs—presumed to be fully converted to GDP lattice—capped by GMPCPP for stability. Using this modiﬁed set-up, we ﬁnd that, as previously reported, EB1 preferentially binds the GTPγS lattice over the GDP lattice (Fig. 3c, d). Under our assay conditions, TPX2 displays a minor but signiﬁcant preference for GTPγS over GDP. In addition, we observe that augmin displays a minor but statistically signiﬁcant preferential localization to the GTPγS over GDP lattice (Fig. 3c, d). Taking all this data together, we ﬁnd that augmin’s primary preference is for more native, compacted lattice instead of the expanded GMPCPP lattice. Additionally, augmin displays a slight preference for GTPγS lattice over GDP lattice, although this preference is less pronounced than the preference for GTPγS over GMPCPP. To conﬁrm that lattice mismatch did not cause distortions to the structure of augmin on the MT, we solved a moderate-resolution structure of T-IIbonsai bound to the GTPγS lattice (Supplementary Figs. 14–16, Supplementary Table 1). At this resolution, approximately

8 Å around augmin (Supplementary Figs. 12d, 16a), we can resolve secondary structure corresponding to T-IIbonsai. We ﬁnd that Haus6’s CH domain directly contacts the GTPγS lattice in a similar manner to the GMPCPP lattice (Supplementary Fig. 16b). Compaction of the GTPγS lattice by comparison to GMPCPP, which comprises both interdimer and intradimer compaction as previously reported28, causes a slight reorientation of the Haus6 CH domain. This reorientation, imposed by a minor reorientation of the α11’ helix of α-tubulin, may underlie augmin’s preference for the more biological compacted lattice state, although at the moderate resolution of the GTPγS structure, this cannot be proved conclusively.

In vitro branching reconstitution provides functional implications for the bipartite MT binding region of augmin We and others have previously shown that branching MT nucleation can be reconstituted in vitro using only augmin and γ-TuRC, while still recapitulating the conserved polarity and shallow branch angles observed in X. laevis meiotic egg extract9–11,14. Therefore, we hypothesized that the MT binding sites of augmin contribute to setting the branch angle. To test this, we performed a series of in vitro branching assays from stabilized MT seeds using recombinant augmin. We expressed and puriﬁed wild type augmin as well as octameric augmin constructs lacking either of its MT binding sites, i.e., lacking either the CH domain of Haus6 (Haus6ΔCH) or the N-terminus of Haus8 (Haus8ΔMTBR). To increase the dwell time of augmin on the MT seeds for long enough to observe branching events, we ﬁrst bound BFPtagged full-length TPX2 at a concentration below its phase boundary32. As discussed above, TPX2 strongly binds to the GMPCPP MT lattice. In addition, it is resistant to washout and helps retain augmin on the lattice (Supplementary Fig. 17) long enough to observe branching events for all constructs tested, even the mutants with reduced MT binding. Once augmin was bound to MTs, we incubated the MT seeds with γ-TuRC puriﬁed from X. laevis egg extract. Finally, ﬂuorescently labeled soluble tubulin and GTP were added to initiate branching from the MT seed (Fig. 4, Supplementary Fig. 18, Supplementary Movie 1). As we have shown previously, augmin octamer and γ-TuRC are sufﬁcient to reconstitute branching from MT seeds14. This minimal reaction recapitulates key features of branching, including a shallow branch angle and conservation of overall MT polarity. However, we previously observed branch angles focused around 15–30° for branching performed with augmin octamer14, despite the fact that the most abundant branch angle observed in Xenopus egg extract is 0 to 15 degrees6,31. When we more closely examined the in vitro branching reaction, we found that the most frequent branch angle is in fact between 0 and 15°, due to the presence of previously-overlooked daughter MTs that form parallel (0–5 degrees) to the MT seed. These parallel MTs were observed both through live imaging as well as by an increase in tubulin intensity at the polymerizing MT plus end in later time points. Parallel MTs are easily distinguishable in our live movies of the wildtype augmin octamer, where kymographs of the plus end shows that a new branched MT nucleates at less than 5 degrees alongside the plus end, while the plus end is polymerizing (Supplementary Fig. 19 and Supplementary Movie 7). Additionally, when analyzing still images from different ﬁelds of view at later time points, quantiﬁcation of several MTs at the plus end revealed a mean intensity approximately 2-fold higher than other branched MTs, indicating that a parallel MT existed at the plus end in addition to the one polymerized from the MT seed (Supplementary Fig. 20). This is likely due to the bundling properties of the Haus8 MTBR, as discussed below. We next tested the effect of the augmin Haus8ΔMTBR and Haus6ΔCH constructs on the branching reaction. Despite their decreased afﬁnity for the MT, both constructs are competent to support the nucleation of daughter MTs from the pre-existing seed, (Fig. 4b, Supplementary Movies 2–5). Discussion In this work, we have reported the cryo-EM structure of an augmin subcomplex, T-IIbonsai, bound to the MT lattice. Surprisingly, this structure displayed no ordered density for the known MT binding N-terminal region of Haus8. Instead, it strongly resembled the structure of NDC80 bound to the MT and revealed a second MT binding site composed of the CH domain of Haus6 in complex with an αβ-tubulin dimer. This interaction between CH domain and MT is critical for augmin to bind the MT with high afﬁnity, as is, to a lesser extent, the Haus8 MTBR. We further found that the augmin complex displays a strong preference for GTPγS-bound MTs over GMPCPP-bound MTs. This spatial preference is the opposite of the strong GMPCPPpreference of the branching factor TPX2. Despite this opposing spatial preference on endogenous-like MTs, we could reconstitute MT branching in vitro using both TPX2 and augmin, along with the MT nucleator γ-TuRC. This allowed us to probe the function of augmin’s two MT binding sites during MT branching. We concluded that both the ordered binding of the Haus6 CH domain, as well as the disordered binding of the Haus8 MTBR, play critical roles in establishing branching geometry and thus in regulating spindle polarity. We were only able to obtain the structure of a relatively small augmin subcomplex on the MT, as the full-length complex proved a poor structural target. However, by combining our prior knowledge of the structure of the full augmin octamer with the structure of T-IIbonsai on the MT, we can arrive at a model of full-length augmin bound to the MT (Fig. 5a). From this model, we observe that the tip of the augmin complex projects approximately 40 nm from the surface of the MT lattice. The disordered Haus8 MTBR, comprising 154 residues, would, at its full extension, be able to extend 54 nm from the MT lattice surface, although AlphaFold3 models (Supplementary Fig. 3) suggest that it will most commonly sample a region extending 19 nm. Depending where on augmin γ-TuRC binds12,13,17,33, augmin thus may be able to capture both soluble γ-TuRC and growing MT branches at a distance of more than a MT diameter, aiding the complex in its role as a γ-TuRC tether. This suggests that there may be a tension at the branch site between, on the one hand, recruiting enough augmin to retain weakly-binding soluble γ-TuRC versus, on the other, leaving enough physical space to accommodate other complexes required for branching. Prior biochemical work12 had suggested that the N-terminal MTBR of Haus8 was insufﬁcient to explain the afﬁnity of augmin for the MT lattice. Our work has borne out this hypothesis, ﬁnding that the CH domain of Haus6 substantially enhances the afﬁnity of X. laevis augmin for the MT (Fig. 5b). However, the function of the dual MT binding regions of augmin is not simply to increase augmin’s ability to bind MTs. The bipartite binding site also functions downstream in organizing the MT branch site and controlling the angle at which the new MT emerges. It is relatively straightforward to explain how the Haus6 CH domain accomplishes this. Our structure suggests that the CH domain binds in an ordered manner to the MT lattice. Thus, deletion of an ordered binding site should cause the augmin complex to become more ﬂexibly attached, and would result in the broader distribution of branching angles that we observe (Fig. 5b). However, the role of the Haus8 MTBR is harder to explain. We observe that this region, although disordered in our structure, is critical to keep MT branch angles shallow. Similarly, divergent interphase and mitotic Haus8 MTBRs have been hypothesized to establish cell-cycle-dependent branch angles in vivo in Arabidopsis34. One possible hypothesis for how Haus8 is acting comes from the ability of the Haus8 MTBR to bundle MTs (Supplementary Fig. 12)18. As discussed above, the Haus8 MTBR might bundle MTs either directly, by interacting with tubulin tails on both preexisting and nascent MTs, or else through indirect means, for example reducing electrostatic repulsion by neutralizing the tubulin tails35,36. Regardless of the mechanism, MT bundling, acting on the nascent MT, could lead to a preference for more acute angles; thus, removal of the MT bundler would lead to wider angles, which is in fact what we observe. While our work answers some outstanding questions about the structure and mechanism of MT branching, it also raises others. In particular, the only major component missing from our model of the branch site is now γ-TuRC. Thus, determining where on the augmin complex γ-TuRC binds will complete our structure of the MT branch. Recent work from two groups has provided clues as to augmin’s interaction with γ-TuRC via the NEDD1 adaptor protein. Recent work using A. thaliana augmin and available in preprint from the Al-Bassam group37 shows that the N-terminal WD40 domain of NEDD1 binds to the top of the T-II arch. This binding location is perhaps surprising, as the NEDD1 WD40 domain will, ﬁrst of all, be located too far from the MT surface when docked onto T-II to provide additional MT binding afﬁnity as has been previously hypothesized11. Secondly, as the WD40 domain is connected to the C-terminus of NEDD1, and thus the remainder of γ-TuRC via a ﬂexible linker, this binding interaction will lead to a ﬂexible, not ﬁxed, linkage between augmin and γ-TuRC that seems unlikely to support branching at a ﬁxed angle. A solution to this conundrum is suggested by a second publication from the Pfeffer and Schiebel groups describing the structure of the C-terminus of NEDD1 bound to the base of the γ-TuRC cone38. Using molecular modeling, the authors predict a second, ﬁxed-orientation interaction between the extreme C-terminus of Haus1, representing the farthest tip of T-III, and the C-terminal 4-helix bundle of NEDD1. Thus, it appears that, just as augmin uses both ordered and ﬂexible interactions to bind the MT, it may also use both ordered and ﬂexible interactions to capture and orient γ-TuRC. Prior work11 has also suggested that multiple augmin complexes may be required at a single branch site. In addition to determining how these augmin complexes could recruit one another and their relative orientations, this also begs the question of why multiple copies of augmin are needed. We have previously observed that binding between a single augmin complex and γ-TuRC in solution

is relatively weak13. Therefore, it is possible that the presence of multiple augmin complexes on the MT would strengthen the interaction with γ-TuRC through the effects of avidity. Secondly, our unexpected ﬁnding that the augmin complex prefers the GTPγS lattice, over both the expanded GMPCPP lattice as well as, to a lesser extent, the GDP lattice, is consistent with augmin’s homology to the plus-tip tracker NDC80, but adds a layer of complexity to another open question, the spatiotemporal control of branching. Prior work has suggested that, on dynamic MTs, augmin does not plus track and in fact prefers older MT lattice11. Therefore, although augmin may thermodynamically prefer the structure of “new” MT lattice, it appears that, in practice, binding of augmin to MTs is driven by kinetic effects to prefer the older, although structurally non-ideal, GDP lattice. In this, augmin is similar to TPX2, which, although under some conditions recognizes the GTP or transition state lattice39, in general accumulates on older lattice through a slow (or biphasic) process1,11,30. In line with this, MT branch sites preferentially form on older MT lattice11,31. Thus, within the spindle, it appears that not only MTs themselves exist within a kinetic, not thermodynamic regime, but similarly the factors that control new MT nucleation, at least via the branching process, are themselves controlled by kinetic considerations. In summary, our structural and biochemical work have established the basis for how augmin binds the MT and how augmin binding to the MT helps to orient new MT branches. This work thus advances our understanding of the MT branch site, which is key to generating spindle MTs and to establishing the structure of the spindle itself.

Cryo-EM data processing Cryo-EM data processing was performed as previously described in ref. 8 using cryoSPARC version 4.4.046. Motion correction was performed using the patch motion correction algorithm, followed by CTF correction using CTFFind version 447. For the GMPCPP structure, approximately 100 micrographs were manually picked, and templates were generated by 2D classiﬁcation. Templates were then used for autopicking using the ﬁlament tracer utility in cryoSPARC. For the GTPγS structure, microtubules were manually picked as ﬁlaments in Relion 3.1.048, and particles were extracted along the ﬁlament length at a separation of 82.5 Å. Particles were sorted using two rounds of 2D classiﬁcation (Supplementary Figs. 6b, 14b), then 13- and 14- protoﬁlament MTs were sorted by heterogeneous reﬁnement from undecorated references. Alignments for the predominant 14- protoﬁlament class were then further reﬁned using the helical reﬁnement and local reﬁnement routines in cryoSPARC (Supplementary Figs. 6c, 14c). Particles from local reﬁnement were then transferred to Frealign version 949,50 for two rounds of seam searching using the protocol previously outlined8,51. Correctly aligned particles were reimported into cryoSPARC, individually CTF-corrected, and locally reﬁned to produce the C1 map (Supplementary Figs. 6d, 14d). For GMPCPP, symmetry expansion was performed using a helical rise of

8.988 Å, a helical twist of −25.75°, and 11-fold symmetrization (to avoid mis-averaging of α, β-tubulin across the microtubule seam). For GTPγS, symmetry expansion was performed using a helical rise of 9.455 Å, a helical twist of −27.69°, and 11-fold symmetrization The symmetry-expanded data set was further reﬁned using a mask around a tubulin dimer (located at the opposite side of the seam) plus augmin density (Supplementary Figs. 6e, 14e). The GMPCPP map was sharpened using both cryoSPARC “Sharpening Tools” with a B-factor of 60 Å2 and using DeepEMhancer with the tightT setting52. The GTPγS map was ﬁltered using cryoSPARC’s “Local Filter” job.

Preparation of functionalized coverslips and imaging chambers We used a previously published method to generate functionalized glass coverslips for TIRF imaging43,61,62. Brieﬂy, coverslips were sonicated in 3 M NaOH followed by Piranha solution (2:3 ratio of 30% w/w H2O2 to sulfuric acid). After washing with MilliQ water, we dried and then treated the coverslips with 3-glycidyloxypropyl trimethoxysilane (GOPTS, cat. # 440167, Sigma) at 75 °C for 30 min. Unreacted GOPTS was removed with two sequential acetone washes, and the coverslips were then dried with nitrogen gas. Between sandwiched coverslips, we melted a powder mix of 9 parts HO-PEG-NH2 and 1 part biotin-CONH- PEG-NH2 by weight (cat. #103000–20 and #133000-25-20, Rapp Polymere, Tübingen, Germany) at 75 °C. We pressed out air bubbles and repeated cycles of 75 °C incubation and pressing. After an overnight incubation at 75 °C, the sandwiches were separated and washed in MilliQ water. These were then spun dry in air and stored at 4 °C for up to 1 month. We made imaging chambers by ﬁrst making a channel on a glass slide with double-sided tape. To this channel, we added 2 mg/mL PLL- γ-PEG (SuSOS AG, Dübendorf, Switzerland) in MilliQ water. After a 20 min incubation, the channel was rinsed thoroughly with MilliQ water and dried with nitrogen gas. Using a diamond pen, functionalized coverslips were cut into quarters. Each quarter piece was then added to the double sided tape on the slide with the functionalized surface facing down. Chambers were made fresh on the day of each experiment.

Tubulin labeling and preparation of double cycled GMPCPP-stabilized MTs Bovine brain tubulin was labeled following prior methods9. Using Alexa568-NHS ester (Invitrogen; A20003) yielded 36–40% labeling efﬁciency. Double cycled GMPCPP-stabilized MTs were made as previously described (42, 63). Brieﬂy, 18 μM unlabeled bovine tubulin supplemented with 1 μM Alexa568 labeled tubulin and 1 μM biotinylated tubulin was polymerized in BRB80 buffer (80 mM PIPES, pH 6.8, 1 mM EGTA, and 1 mM MgCl2) in the presence of 1 mM GMPCPP for 1 h at 37 °C. After 1 h, the MT seed mixture was centrifuged at 17,000 x g at room temperature for 15 min. The remaining pellet was then resuspended in cold BRB80 and left on ice to depolymerize for 20 min, followed by a second round of polymerization with 1 mM GMPCPP for 1 h at 37 °C. After 1 h, the mixture was centrifuged again at 17,000 x g at room temperature for 15 min. The supernatant was removed, and the

Preparation of subtilisin-cleaved, GMPCPP MT seeds Single cycled, GMPCPP-stabilized MT seeds were ﬁrst prepared. Brieﬂy, 18 μM unlabeled bovine tubulin supplemented with 1 μM Alexa568 labeled tubulin and 1 μM biotinylated tubulin was polymerized in BRB80 buffer (80 mM PIPES, pH 6.8, 1 mM EGTA, and 1 mM MgCl2) in the presence of 1 mM GMPCPP for 1 h at 37 °C. After 1 h, the MT seed mixture was centrifuged at 17,000 x g at room temperature for 15 min. The supernatant was removed and the pellet was resuspended in warm BRB80 supplemented with 1 mM GMPCPP. The MTs were then incubated with 100 ug/ml Subtilisin A, and incubated at 37 °C for 1 h. 2 mM PMSF was then added to quench the reaction, and the seeds were spun down at 17,000 × g at room temperature for 15 min. The supernatant was removed, and the pellet was washed one time with BRB80 to remove any additional Subtilisin A. The ﬁnal pellet was resuspended in warm BRB80, and used immediately for TIRF microscopy experiments.

The seeds were pelleted by centrifugation at 17,000 ×g at room temperature for 15 min, then resuspended in 10% Alexa568 labeled 50 μM tubulin in modiﬁed BRB80 buffer containing 0.2 mM MgCl2 and 1 mM guanosine 5’-O-[γ-thio]triphosphate (GTPγS) (pre-incubated on ice for 5 min). The mixture was then polymerized for 1 h at 37 °C. These seeds were pelleted again by the same means and resuspended in 0.2 mM MgCl2 BRB80 supplemented with 1 mM DTT. To prepare a 1:1 mixture of labeled GTPγS and GDP seeds, we modiﬁed the above protocol to produce GMPCPP-Atto-647N GTPγS seeds by omitting ﬂuorescently labeled tubulin from the ﬁrst GMPCPP polymerization step and substituting 10% Atto-647N-labeled tubulin for Alexa568-labeled tubulin in the second GTPγS polymerization step. We produced GMPCPP-capped Alexa568-labeled GDP seeds in the following way. 20 μM bovine brain tubulin with 10% Alexa568-labeled tubulin and 10% biotinylated tubulin in BRB80 supplemented with 15% v/v glycerol were incubated on ice for 5 min then polymerized in the presence of 1 mM GTP at 37 °C for 45 min. TIRF imaging and image analysis Total internal reﬂection ﬂuorescence (TIRF) microscopy was performed with a Nikon TiE microscope using a 100 × 1.49 NA objective. Andor Zyla sCMOS camera was used for acquisition, with a ﬁeld of view of 165.1 × 139.3 µm. 2 × 2 binned, multi-color images were acquired using NIS-Elements version 5.02.01-Build 1270 (Nikon). All adjustable imaging parameters (exposure time, laser intensity, and TIRF angle) were kept the same within experiments. For MT nucleation assays in vitro, the TIRF objective was warmed to 33 °C using an objective heater (Bioptechs, 150819–13). For all time-lapse imaging, one multi-color image was taken at the beginning of the experiment followed by collection of time-lapse images on the 647 nm channel every 2 s for 10 min. After the time lapse was collected, another multi-color image was taken. For still images of augmin binding and branched MT nucleation experiments, an additional 15–30 multi-color images were collected. Brightness and contrast were optimized individually for display. Images used for the quantiﬁcation of MT binding were analyzed using FIJI/ImageJ. Background subtraction was performed using the Subtract Background command on the MAP channel. To segment MTs, the tubulin signal was ﬁrst thresholded via the Otsu method. MTs were isolated from the mask by setting the minimum particle area as 1 or 2 μm2. Average ﬂuorescent signals per pixel, for the MT or for bound proteins, were calculated for each MT. The average intensity from the reverse mask of the entire ﬁeld of view was subtracted from the average intensity on each MT. For branching MT nucleation experiments in vitro, MTs were counted manually using time-lapse experiments, and multiple aspects of the data were taken into account to exclude MTs of ambiguous origin. In the case where branched MTs were quantiﬁed from still images, the MTs were counted manually and only included in the analysis if there was a clear distinction between the plus and minus end of the MT. Additionally, branched MTs were excluded from analysis if two microtubule seeds were close to each other on the glass coverslip, and the origin of the daughter MT was ambiguous in a still image. Branched MTs were also excluded if there was a possibility of what we term a crossing event, where a spontaneously nucleated MT could be above the immobilized seed. In the case that the origin of the branched MT was still ambiguous, kymographs were prepared from the live movies to detect which MTs were true branches vs. spontaneously nucleated (Supplementary Fig. 22). Branch angles were measured manually using FIJI/ImageJ. For nearly parallel branch angles of <5 degrees, kymographs were made of the MT plus ends to show that a second MT was growing in addition to the polymerizing MT end (Supplementary Fig. 19, Supplementary Movie 6). To quantify parallel branch angles in the still images, the mean intensity of the plus end was quantiﬁed to show that the intensity was twice of that expected if there was only a single MT polymerizing from the plus end (Supplementary Fig. 20). The branch angle distributions were plotted as histograms in Prism.
